title: Manage Secure AI Development Lifecycle (AIDLC) and Change Management
intro: Making security part of how AI is built and changed: integrating security activities and automated gates across the AI lifecycle and its MLOps and LLMOps pipelines; adapting environmental controls such as separation, least privilege and secure API integration; managing every behaviour-changing change, from models and datasets to prompts and retrieval, through versioning and release manifests; and rolling out changes in stages with tested rollback procedures.
objectives: Integrate security activities and automated gates into every stage of the AI lifecycle, for both MLOps and LLMOps
Adapt separation, least privilege and secure API integration to AI research, development, training and production environments
Apply change management to models, datasets, retrieval, prompts, guardrails and tools, using versioning and release manifests
Plan staged rollouts such as shadow and canary deployments, with pre-agreed triggers and rollback of the whole release bundle

sections.title: Security across the AI development lifecycle

blocks.title: Building security into MLOps and LLMOps

scenes.title: Building security into MLOps and LLMOps
scenes.sub: Security across the AI development lifecycle
scenes.say: Security bolted on at the end of an AI project is expensive and weak. Security built into every stage of the lifecycle, and automated in the pipelines, is cheaper and much harder to bypass. | This video covers integrating security across the AI development lifecycle, in both MLOps and LLMOps.

scenes.title: The secure AI development lifecycle
scenes.intro: Each stage has its own security activities.

stages.label: Plan and design
stages.d: Use case risk, threat model, requirements.

scenes.say: The secure AI development lifecycle has six stages, each with its own security activities. | Plan and design: assess the use case’s risk, threat model the architecture and set security requirements. | Data: verify provenance and consent, validate quality and protect sensitive data. | Build and train: write secure code, train in isolated environments and record lineage. | Evaluate: test quality, safety, fairness and security against agreed thresholds. | Release: sign artefacts, approve according to risk and roll out in stages. | Operate and retire: monitor, respond to incidents and decommission securely. | Then the cycle repeats, because every retraining or major change goes round again.

scenes.title: MLOps and LLMOps
scenes.say: MLOps and LLMOps share principles but differ in emphasis. | In MLOps, the main artefact is usually a model you train yourself. In LLMOps, it is often a model you consume from a provider or open source. | MLOps changes come mostly from data and retraining. LLMOps changes come from prompts, retrieval sources and tools, often weekly. | MLOps testing focuses on accuracy, drift and fairness. LLMOps adds safety, injection resistance and grounding. | And LLMOps has extra assets to secure: prompt templates, retrieval indexes and guardrail configurations.

scenes.title: Security gates in an AI pipeline
scenes.say: Here is how security gates fit into an AI pipeline. Every change starts as a commit: code, prompt templates and configuration all live in version control. | Continuous integration scans for secrets, code weaknesses and vulnerable dependencies. | Artefact checks scan model files for unsafe formats and verify dataset hashes and licences. | An evaluation gate runs safety, security and quality suites, and blocks the release if thresholds aren’t met. | Passing artefacts are signed, with provenance, and approved according to risk. | And deployment is staged, with admission checks that accept only signed, approved artefacts.

scenes.title: Frameworks for a secure AI lifecycle

items.d: Principles from design to end of life

scenes.say: Six frameworks help structure a secure AI lifecycle. | NIST special publication 800-218A, a profile of the secure software development framework for generative AI and foundation models. | The UK’s AI Cyber Security Code of Practice, with principles from secure design to end of life. | ETSI technical specification 104 223, which turned those principles into baseline requirements. | ISO/IEC 5338, which defines AI system life cycle processes. | Google’s Secure AI Framework. | And the OWASP AI Exchange, an open body of guidance on AI security.

items: Security activities at every lifecycle stage
LLMOps adds prompts, indexes, guardrails and tools to secure
Automate gates: scans, evaluations, signing, admission
Use SSDF 800-218A, UK Code, ETSI, ISO/IEC 5338
scenes.say: To recap. | Build security activities into every stage of the AI lifecycle, from planning to retirement. | Remember that LLMOps adds prompts, retrieval indexes, guardrails and tools to the assets you must secure. | Automate the gates: scans, evaluations, signing and admission checks. | And structure the programme with frameworks such as NIST SP 800-218A, the UK Code of Practice, ETSI TS 104 223 and ISO/IEC 5338.

blocks.md:
### Security activities by lifecycle stage
| Stage | Key security activities |
|---|---|
| **Plan and design** | Use case risk assessment and tiering (Module 2.3); threat modelling (Module 6.1); security, privacy and safety requirements; architecture review (Module 4.1) |
| **Data** | Provenance and licensing checks; consent and lawful basis; validation and poisoning defences; minimisation, masking and access control (Domain 3) |
| **Build and train** | Secure coding for pipelines and agents; isolated training environments; pinned and scanned dependencies; lineage and experiment tracking (Module 4.3) |
| **Evaluate** | Quality, robustness, fairness and safety evaluations; security testing and red teaming (Module 6.4); documented results in the model card |
| **Release** | Signed artefacts with provenance (SLSA); risk-based approval; admission control; staged rollout with rollback (Section 4) |
| **Operate** | Telemetry, detection and response (Domain 5); configuration and drift control (Module 5.1); vulnerability management (Module 5.4) |
| **Retire** | Secure decommissioning and disposal (Module 5.7) |

### MLOps and LLMOps security
- **MLOps** (operations for trained models): feature and dataset versioning, training pipeline integrity, model registries, drift monitoring and retraining controls.
- **LLMOps** (operations for applications built on large language models): **prompt management** (versioned, reviewed templates), **evaluation harnesses** for safety, injection and grounding, **guardrail configuration**, **RAG ingestion and index pipelines**, **tool and agent definitions**, and **provider version management**.
- In both, treat every artefact that changes behaviour as code: versioned, reviewed, tested and deployed through the pipeline.

### Frameworks
- **NIST SP 800-218A** (July 2024) adds AI-specific practices to the Secure Software Development Framework for generative AI and dual-use foundation models, such as protecting training data and model weights and testing for AI-specific vulnerabilities.
- **The UK AI Cyber Security Code of Practice** (January 2025) sets 13 principles across five phases: secure design, secure development, secure deployment, secure maintenance and secure end of life. **ETSI TS 104 223** (2025) built on it to create baseline security requirements for AI models and systems.
- **ISO/IEC 5338** defines life cycle processes for AI systems, based on ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 and 12207.
- **Google SAIF** and the **OWASP AI Exchange** provide practical control guidance (Module 4.1).

blocks.title: Which lifecycle stage?
pairs: Checking the licence and provenance of a scraped dataset
Running injection and jailbreak suites before release
Requiring signed model artefacts at deployment
Threat modelling a proposed agent architecture

blocks.title: The fast-moving assistant team
blocks.md: A product team ships changes to its customer assistant several times a week. Code goes through CI with secret scanning, but new model versions are downloaded from a public hub and loaded directly, evaluation is "a quick try in the playground", and prompt changes are pasted into production by whoever is on duty. Last month, a prompt change caused the assistant to reveal internal pricing rules.

q.q: Which improvement would MOST reduce the risk of similar problems?
o: Slow releases down to once a quarter, so each one can be reviewed by hand
Pipeline gates for models and prompts: artefact scans, evaluations, signing, approval
Ask the person on duty to double-check prompt changes before pasting them in
Stop using models from public hubs and train every model in-house instead
q.why: Automated gates for every behaviour-changing artefact catch unsafe models and prompts before production, without stopping frequent releases. Quarterly releases sacrifice agility, self-checks are unreliable, and training everything in-house is disproportionate.

blocks.title: Lifecycle questions
blocks.md: Expect the best answer to put security **into every stage** and **into the pipeline** as automated, enforceable gates (scans, evaluations, signing, admission), rather than relying on a manual review at the end. For LLM applications, remember that **prompts, retrieval indexes, guardrails and tool definitions** are artefacts that need versioning, testing and approval too.

q.q: An LLM application team changes its system prompt and retrieval sources weekly, directly in production, while its model releases go through a formal pipeline. What is the MOST important improvement?
o: Freeze all prompt and retrieval changes, so the application never changes after launch
Manage prompts and retrieval configuration as code, through the same tested pipeline
Ask the team to email a summary of each weekly change to the security team
Move the model releases out of the pipeline so that both are handled the same way
q.why: Prompts and retrieval settings change behaviour as much as model releases, so they need versioning, testing and approval through the pipeline. Freezing them blocks legitimate improvement, emails don’t control anything, and weakening the model process makes things worse.

scenes.title: Keeping AI environments apart
scenes.sub: Separation, least privilege and secure API integration
scenes.say: AI development is messy by nature: notebooks, experiments, shared GPU clusters and copies of data everywhere. Without clear environmental controls, experiments leak into production and production data leaks into experiments. | This video covers adapting environmental controls for AI: separation, least privilege and secure API integration.

scenes.title: Separated AI environments
scenes.say: Separate AI work into distinct environments. A research sandbox for exploration, using synthetic or masked data rather than raw production data. | Development, with no access to production secrets or systems. | Training, in isolated environments that only use approved, versioned datasets. | The model registry is the controlled bridge: only registered, signed versions move onwards, so everything later can be traced and verified. | Staging, where production-like tests and evaluations run on the registered version. | And production, where changes arrive only through the pipeline, never by hand.

scenes.title: Least privilege in AI environments
scenes.say: Least privilege needs adapting for AI environments. | Notebooks need authentication, and nobody should share an administrator account. Exposed notebook servers are a common route in. | GPU clusters need per-project access and quotas. | Write access to the model registry should belong to pipelines, while people read. | Training data access should cover approved datasets only, granted just in time. | Secrets should be vaulted, scoped and short-lived, never pasted into notebooks. | And outbound network access should be limited to allow-listed destinations, so a compromised job can’t send data anywhere.

scenes.title: Integrating with AI APIs securely
scenes.say: Integrations with model providers, tools and data APIs need care. | The risky pattern is one shared key embedded in code. The secure pattern is per-service, scoped credentials that are rotated, ideally short-lived tokens. | Risky: calls over the public internet, from hosts that can reach anywhere. Secure: private endpoints where available, and egress allow-lists. | Risky: sending everything, with no agreement on what the provider keeps. Secure: minimised data and contractually agreed retention. | And risky: unlimited calls. Secure: quotas, time-outs and validation of every response against an expected schema.

scenes.title: AI-specific environment risks
scenes.say: Six risks are especially common in AI environments. | Exposed notebook servers and experiment dashboards, which internet scanners find quickly. | Copies of production data in development, outside production’s controls. | Unsafe model files from public hubs, which can run code when loaded. | Code-executing agents, which need sandboxes with no access to secrets or internal networks. | Shared GPU tenancy, where workloads must be isolated from each other. | And keys pasted into notebooks, then committed to repositories or shared by mistake.

scenes.title: How an exposed notebook becomes a breach

events.d: Notebook opened to the internet, no login
Cloud credentials in cells and variables
GPU bill spikes; data already copied

scenes.say: Here is a pattern seen repeatedly in real incidents. | A researcher opens a notebook server to the internet for convenience, with no login required. | Within hours, automated scanners find it. | An attacker uses the notebook’s built-in terminal to run code on the server. | They harvest cloud credentials left in notebook cells and environment variables, and use them to reach data and other systems. | The breach is noticed days later, when the GPU bill spikes from cryptocurrency mining. By then, the data has already been copied.

items: Separate research, dev, training, staging and production
Move models only through the registry and pipeline
Least privilege for notebooks, GPUs, registries, data, secrets, egress
Secure API integration: scoped credentials, private paths, limits
scenes.say: To recap. | Separate research, development, training, staging and production environments. | Move models between them only through the registry and the pipeline. | Apply least privilege to notebooks, GPU clusters, registries, data, secrets and outbound access. | And integrate with AI APIs using scoped credentials, private network paths, minimised data and strict limits.

blocks.md:
### Environment separation for AI
| Environment | Purpose | Key controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Research sandbox** | Exploration and prototyping | Synthetic, sampled or masked data; no production credentials; egress controls; time-limited |
| **Development** | Building pipelines, agents and applications | Code in version control; secrets from a vault; no production data or systems |
| **Training** | Producing models from approved data | Isolated compute; approved, versioned datasets; pinned dependencies; lineage capture (Module 4.3) |
| **Staging** | Production-like testing and evaluation | Same configuration as production; evaluation and security gates; test data |
| **Production** | Serving users | Changes only through the pipeline; signed artefacts; monitoring; break-glass access only (Module 5.1) |

The **model registry** is the controlled bridge: models move from training to staging to production only as registered, signed and approved versions (Module 3.5).

### Least privilege, adapted
- **Notebooks and workbenches:** authenticated access, no shared administrator accounts, no inbound exposure to the internet, idle shutdown, and secrets injected at runtime rather than written in cells.
- **Compute:** per-project GPU access and quotas; isolation between tenants and workloads; ephemeral training jobs with their own identities.
- **Registries and artefact stores:** pipeline identities write; people read; promotion requires approval.
- **Data:** access to approved datasets only, granted just in time and logged; production personal data stays in production unless a documented, approved exception applies (Module 3.4).
- **Egress:** allow-lists for package registries, model hubs and provider endpoints; block everything else by default.

### Secure API integration
- **Credentials:** per-service, least-privilege keys or, better, short-lived tokens from workload identity federation (Module 4.5); never in code or prompts.
- **Network:** private connectivity to providers where offered; TLS everywhere; mutual TLS for internal services.
- **Data:** minimise what is sent; mask personal data where possible (Module 5.2); agree retention and training use in contracts (Module 2.5).
- **Robustness:** time-outs, retries with limits, circuit breakers, quotas, and validation of responses against schemas, because model and tool outputs are untrusted (Module 3.5).

blocks.title: Environment terms
cards: An isolated environment for experiments, using synthetic or masked data and no production credentials.
Moving a registered, approved model version from one environment to the next through the pipeline.
A list of the only external destinations a workload may connect to.
Issuing short-lived credentials to workloads based on their identity, instead of long-lived keys.
A connection to a provider’s service over a private network path rather than the public internet.

blocks.title: Environment questions
blocks.md: Look for **separated environments** joined only by the **registry and pipeline**, **least privilege** adapted to notebooks, GPU clusters, registries and data, **no production personal data in development** without an approved exception, and **secure API integration** (scoped, short-lived credentials; private paths; egress allow-lists; response validation).

q.q: Data scientists copy full production customer data into a shared notebook environment to experiment with a new model. What is the BEST alternative?
o: Allow it, provided the data scientists sign a confidentiality agreement first
Use synthetic or masked data in an isolated sandbox, with exceptions approved
Move the experiments directly into production, where the data already lives
Delete the notebook environment, and ban experimentation with customer data
q.why: Synthetic or masked data in an isolated sandbox supports experimentation without spreading production personal data, and any genuine need goes through an approved exception. Agreements don’t reduce exposure, experimenting in production is risky, and banning experimentation blocks legitimate work.

scenes.title: Every change that changes behaviour
scenes.say: In traditional systems, behaviour changes when code changes. In AI systems, behaviour also changes when data, prompts, retrieval sources or a provider’s model change, often with no code change at all. | This video covers AI-specific change management, built on versioning models, datasets and retrieval.

scenes.title: What counts as a change

items.d: New weights, fine-tune or provider version

scenes.say: Six kinds of change alter an AI system’s behaviour, and all of them need change management. | A new model version: new weights, a fine-tune, or a different provider version. | A new dataset version, for training or for evaluation. | Changes to retrieval: the index, its sources or its embedding model. | Changes to prompts and templates. | Changes to guardrails: policies, thresholds or classifiers. | And changes to tools and permissions: new tools, wider scopes or more autonomy.

scenes.title: A versioned release bundle
scenes.code:
release: support-assistant 2026.11.2
model: support-llm v3.4  sha256:5c1e...
dataset: tickets-ft v12  sha256:a91b...
prompt: system v27  (reviewed: PR 1142)
index: kb-2026-11-01  embed: e5-v2
guardrails: policy v9  injection>0.85
tools: crm.read, ticket.update
evals: safety 99.2% / quality 91.4%
approved: model owner, security

notes.d: Every behaviour-changing component, pinned and hashed.
A single identifier for the whole combination.
Exact versions and hashes, with review references.
Index snapshot, embedding model, policy and tool scopes.
Evaluation results that justify the release.
Who approved, in line with the risk tier.

scenes.say: The core tool of AI change management is the release manifest: one record that pins every behaviour-changing component. | It gives the whole combination a single release identifier. | It pins the model, the fine-tuning dataset and the system prompt to exact versions, with hashes and review references. | It records the retrieval index snapshot and embedding model, the guardrail policy and thresholds, and the tools the agent may use. | It includes the evaluation results that justify the release. | And it records who approved it. With this, you can reproduce, compare and roll back any release as a unit.

scenes.title: Change classes for AI
scenes.say: Classify AI changes so effort matches risk. | A standard change follows a pre-approved pattern, such as a scheduled index refresh from approved sources. A normal change, such as a new model or a new tool, needs its own approval. An emergency change, such as disabling a harmful tool, has to happen fast. | Standard changes are pre-approved. Normal changes get risk-based sign-off. Emergency changes use pre-agreed on-call authority. | Standard changes pass automated checks. Normal changes run full evaluation suites. And emergency changes are reviewed afterwards, as Module 5.1 described.

scenes.title: A normal AI change
scenes.say: A normal AI change follows six steps. A request states what will change, why, and the system’s risk tier. | Impact analysis considers behaviour, data, users and any regulatory implications, such as a substantial modification to a high-risk system. | The candidate is evaluated against the current version, on the same suites, so differences are visible. | Approval follows the risk tier. | The release goes out in stages, with its manifest. | And the registry, model card and change log are updated, so anyone can see what changed, when and why.

items: Models, data, retrieval, prompts, guardrails and tools are all changes
Pin every component in a versioned release manifest
Standard, normal and emergency classes match effort to risk
Compare with the current version; approve by risk; record
scenes.say: To recap. | Treat changes to models, data, retrieval, prompts, guardrails and tools as changes. | Pin every behaviour-changing component in a versioned release manifest. | Use standard, normal and emergency change classes, so effort matches risk. | And evaluate each candidate against the current version, approve according to risk, and record everything.

blocks.md:
### Versioning everything that changes behaviour
| Component | How to version | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Models** | Registry versions with hashes and signatures; pinned provider versions (Module 3.5) | Reproduce, compare and roll back behaviour |
| **Datasets** | Immutable, content-hashed versions with manifests (Module 3.3) | Trace models to their data; investigate poisoning |
| **Retrieval** | Index snapshots, source lists and embedding model versions | Restore clean indexes; explain answers |
| **Prompts** | Templates in version control, reviewed like code | Explain and reverse behaviour changes |
| **Guardrails** | Policies and thresholds as configuration code (Module 5.1) | Prevent silent loosening |
| **Tools and agents** | Tool definitions, scopes and autonomy settings in configuration | Control agency changes (Module 4.6) |
| **Evaluations** | Versioned test suites and results | Compare releases fairly over time |

### Change management practices
- **A release manifest** pins all of the above for each release, so the combination can be reproduced, compared and rolled back as a unit.
- **Change classes:** standard (pre-approved, low-risk patterns), normal (assessed and approved by risk tier) and emergency (fast, with review afterwards).
- **Impact analysis:** expected behaviour change, data and privacy impact, affected users, and regulatory implications. Under the EU AI Act, a **substantial modification** to a high-risk system can trigger a new conformity assessment.
- **Comparative evaluation:** run the candidate and the current version on the same suites, including safety, security, fairness and quality, and review the differences (Module 5.6).
- **Provider-driven change:** treat provider model updates and retirements as changes too; pin versions and test replacements before switching (Module 5.1).
- **Records:** update the registry, model card, AIBOM and change log; link the change to its request, approvals and evidence (ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A 8.32 covers change management).

blocks.title: Assessing a provider model upgrade
items: Raise the change
Record the current and proposed model versions, the reason (for example, a scheduled retirement) and the system’s risk tier.
Analyse impact
Identify affected prompts, output formats, guardrails, downstream parsers and regulatory obligations.
Evaluate side by side
Run safety, security, quality and fairness suites on both versions with the same prompts and data, and compare.
Adjust and re-test
Tune prompts or guardrails where behaviour changed, and re-run the suites.
Approve and stage
Approve by risk tier, update the release manifest, and roll out in stages with the old version kept as the rollback point.

blocks.title: Which change class fits?
pairs: A scheduled nightly refresh of the index from approved sources
Giving an agent a new tool that can issue refunds
Disabling a tool that an attacker is actively abusing
Moving to a new provider model version
Loosening a guardrail threshold to reduce complaints

blocks.title: Change management questions
blocks.md: The key idea: **anything that changes behaviour is a change**, including prompts, retrieval sources, guardrail thresholds, tools and provider model versions. Strong answers use **versioning and release manifests**, **change classes matched to risk**, **comparative evaluation** against the current version and **records** in the registry and model card. "No code changed, so no change control was needed" is a trap.

q.q: A team switches its retrieval system to a new embedding model and rebuilds the index, without any change request, because "no application code changed". What is the MAIN concern?
o: The new embedding model may use more storage than the previous one
Retrieval changed with no impact analysis, evaluation or rollback point
Embedding models can only be changed by the original model provider
Rebuilding the index should always be done at weekends to avoid disruption
q.why: Changing the embedding model changes what is retrieved and therefore what the system says, so it needs impact analysis, comparative evaluation, a versioned rollback point and approval. Storage, provider rules and timing are secondary.

blocks.title: Releasing AI a little at a time

scenes.title: Releasing AI a little at a time
scenes.say: No test suite captures everything real users will do. Staged rollouts let a new AI version meet real traffic gradually, with automatic brakes if it misbehaves. | This video covers staged rollout patterns, such as canary deployments, and the rollback procedures that make them safe.

scenes.title: Staged rollout patterns

items.d: Runs on real inputs; users see nothing
A small share of real traffic first

scenes.say: Six patterns support staged rollouts. | Shadow deployment: the new version runs on real inputs, but users never see its outputs, so you can compare it safely. | Canary: a small share of real traffic goes to the new version first. | A/B testing: versions are compared on real outcomes. | Blue-green: two complete environments, with an instant switch between them. | Feature flags: capabilities, such as a new agent tool, are turned on for chosen groups. | And rings: staff first, then pilot customers, then everyone.

scenes.title: A canary with automatic rollback
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative share of responses flagged by safety classifiers
scenes.say: Here is an illustrative canary. The current version’s safety flag rate sits steadily below one per cent. | The canary, serving five per cent of traffic, starts similarly, then climbs from the second hour. | When it crosses the agreed rollback trigger of two per cent, automation routes all traffic back to the current version within minutes, and the team investigates. Only five per cent of users were exposed, for a short time.

scenes.title: A rollback procedure
scenes.say: A rollback procedure has six steps. It starts with a trigger: a metric breaching its threshold, or a decision by the model owner. | Traffic is routed back to the last good release. | The whole release bundle is restored, not just the model: the prompt, index and configuration that went with it. | State is handled: in-flight sessions, agent memory written by the new version, and any data or schema changes. | The team verifies that metrics have returned to normal. | And the rollback is recorded and reviewed, so the problem is understood before the next attempt.

scenes.title: What to watch during a rollout
scenes.say: Rollouts need agreed signals and triggers before they start. | Safety signals: safety classifier flags, refusals and injection detections, triggering when they rise above the baseline band. | Quality signals: grounding scores, task success and user feedback, triggering when they fall below thresholds. | Operational signals: latency, errors and cost per request. | And business signals: escalations to humans, complaints and conversions, where a significant change prompts a pause.

items: Shadow, canary, A/B, blue-green, feature flags, rings
Agree signals and rollback triggers before rollout
Roll back the whole bundle, and handle state
Test rollback before you need it
scenes.say: To recap. | Use staged patterns: shadow, canary, A/B testing, blue-green, feature flags and rings. | Agree the signals and rollback triggers before the rollout starts. | Roll back the whole release bundle, and handle state such as sessions, memory and data changes. | And test the rollback procedure before you need it.

blocks.md:
### Staged rollout patterns
| Pattern | How it works | Strengths | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Shadow** | New version processes real inputs; outputs are logged, not shown | Zero user exposure; realistic comparison | No side effects allowed: shadow agents must not act |
| **Canary** | A small percentage of traffic goes to the new version | Real feedback with limited exposure | Choose a representative slice; enough volume for signals |
| **A/B test** | Traffic split to compare outcomes | Measures real impact | Needs ethical and privacy review when outcomes affect people |
| **Blue-green** | Two full environments; switch traffic between them | Instant cutover and rollback | Cost; state and data compatibility |
| **Feature flags** | Capabilities enabled per user group | Fine-grained control, such as new agent tools | Flag sprawl; flags need ownership and removal |
| **Rings** | Internal staff, then pilots, then general availability | Gradual widening of exposure | Staff behaviour may differ from customers |

### Rollback procedures for AI
- **Roll back the bundle:** model, prompt, guardrails, retrieval index and tool configuration from the release manifest (Section 3). Rolling back only the model can leave an incompatible prompt or index.
- **Automate triggers:** agreed thresholds on safety, quality, operational and business signals switch traffic back automatically (Module 5.7 circuit breakers).
- **Handle state:** in-flight sessions, agent memory and notes written by the new version, cached answers, and data or schema migrations. Design changes to be **backward compatible**, so rollback doesn’t corrupt data.
- **Hosted models:** keep the previous model version available until the new one is proven; providers retire versions on schedules, so plan ahead (Module 5.7).
- **Practise:** test rollbacks in staging and game days, and measure how long they take (Module 4.4).
- **Learn:** record why a rollout failed, and fix the cause before trying again (Module 5.7).

blocks.title: The big-bang upgrade
blocks.md: A retailer plans to switch its customer assistant from one model version to a new one for all customers at 9am on Black Friday, its busiest day. The new version passed offline evaluations. There is no canary, the previous version’s configuration has been deleted to "keep things tidy", and nobody has defined what would trigger a rollback.

q.q: What should the security lead recommend?
o: Proceed as planned, because the new version passed its offline evaluations
Restore the previous bundle, define triggers, and canary on a quieter day
Delay the upgrade indefinitely, until a perfect evaluation suite exists
Proceed, but ask customers to report any problems through a survey
q.why: A rollback point, agreed triggers and a canary at low-risk times make the upgrade reversible and limit exposure. Offline evaluations don’t capture everything, indefinite delay isn’t practical, and surveys are too slow.

blocks.title: Rollout questions
blocks.md: Prefer **staged rollouts** (shadow, canary, rings, flags) with **pre-agreed rollback triggers** and **automated rollback** of the **whole release bundle**. Remember **shadow agents must not take real actions**, and that **state** (sessions, memory, data migrations) complicates rollback. A big-bang release with no rollback point is the classic wrong answer.

q.q: A team wants to test a new agent version on real traffic in shadow mode. What is the MOST important precaution?
o: Show the shadow agent’s answers to users, so their feedback can be collected
Ensure the shadow agent can’t take real actions, such as sending emails or payments
Give the shadow agent broader permissions, so that it can be tested much more fully
Run the shadow agent only at night, when fewer users are online
q.why: Shadow mode compares outputs without side effects. A shadow agent that can act would cause real, duplicated or unapproved actions. Showing outputs defeats shadow mode, broader permissions add risk, and timing doesn’t remove side effects.

quiz.q: What does LLMOps add to traditional MLOps?
o: Faster GPU clusters for training very large models from scratch
Managing prompts, evaluations, guardrails and RAG pipelines
A ban on using any models from external providers or open source
Manual human approval of every individual user request
quiz.why: Applications built on language models change through prompts, retrieval and guardrails as much as through models, so these become managed artefacts.

quiz.q: Why should evaluation gates be automated in the AI pipeline?
o: Automated gates remove the need for any security testing elsewhere
Releases that fail agreed thresholds are blocked consistently
Manual reviews are prohibited for AI models under the EU AI Act
Automation makes models more accurate during training
quiz.why: Automated gates apply the same thresholds to every release, and can’t be skipped under deadline pressure.

o: A technical standard for encrypting model weights when stored at rest
An AI-specific profile of the Secure Software Development Framework
A list of approved generative AI providers for US agencies
A testing tool for prompt injection vulnerabilities
quiz.why: SP 800-218A adds practices for generative AI and dual-use foundation models to NIST’s SSDF.

quiz.q: Why should models move between environments only through the registry?
o: The registry compresses models, so they deploy much faster
Everything in production stays traceable, verified and approved
Environments can’t share network connections of any kind
Registries are required before models can be trained on GPUs
quiz.why: A single controlled path means every production model is a registered, signed and approved version.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of copying production personal data into development notebooks?
o: Notebooks run more slowly when they process real data
The data leaves production’s controls and spreads to more people
Development environments can’t store data larger than a gigabyte
Models trained in notebooks are always less accurate
quiz.why: Development environments have weaker controls and wider access, so copies multiply exposure; use synthetic or masked data instead.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST secures integration with a model provider’s API?
o: One shared key embedded in the application code for simplicity
Scoped, short-lived credentials over private paths, with response validation
Sending all the data available, so the model has the most context possible
Allowing the integration host to reach any internet destination
quiz.why: Scoped, short-lived credentials limit misuse, private paths reduce exposure, and validating responses treats model output as untrusted.

quiz.q: Which change requires AI change management even though no application code changes?
o: Restarting the serving containers during routine maintenance
Switching the retrieval index to a new embedding model
Adding a new dashboard to the monitoring tool
Renewing the TLS certificate on the API gateway
quiz.why: A new embedding model changes what is retrieved, and therefore what the system says.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a release manifest for an AI system?
o: To advertise new features to customers, in the release notes
To pin every behaviour-changing component, for reproducibility
To record which engineers worked on the release, for payroll purposes
To replace the need for any evaluation before release
quiz.why: Pinning model, data, prompt, index, guardrail and tool versions lets a release be reproduced, compared and rolled back as a unit.

quiz.q: What is a standard change in AI change management?
o: Any change made by a senior engineer, whatever its risk
A pre-approved, low-risk change that follows an agreed pattern
A change that must always be approved by the board of directors
A change that bypasses all testing, to save time in urgent cases
quiz.why: Standard changes, such as scheduled index refreshes from approved sources, are pre-approved because their risk is understood and controlled.

quiz.q: What makes shadow deployment different from a canary release?
o: Shadow deployments only run at weekends, when traffic is lower
In shadow mode, users never see any of the new version’s outputs
Shadow deployments skip monitoring, to avoid slowing users down
Canary releases never use real traffic, only synthetic test data
quiz.why: Shadow mode compares behaviour on real inputs with no user exposure; a canary exposes a small share of real users.

quiz.q: Why should a rollback restore the whole release bundle, not just the model?
o: Restoring only the model is always slower than restoring everything
An old model with a new prompt or index may behave unpredictably
Regulators prohibit rolling back models without rolling back logs
Bundles are smaller than individual models
quiz.why: Behaviour depends on the combination, so the last known-good combination is what must be restored.

quiz.q: When should rollback triggers be agreed?
o: After the first complaints arrive from customers
Before the rollout starts, as part of the release plan
Only after an incident has been declared by the SOC
At the end of the year, during the annual review
quiz.why: Triggers agreed in advance allow automatic, uncontested rollback when signals breach their limits.

exam.q: A company’s AI projects run security reviews only in the week before launch, and findings often delay releases by months. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Skip the reviews for projects that are behind schedule
Build security into every lifecycle stage, with automated gates
Hire an external firm to perform the same review in less time
Move the review to after launch, so it no longer delays releases
exam.why: Security built into each stage finds issues early, when they are cheap to fix, and automated gates keep releases moving. Skipping, outsourcing the same late review or reviewing after launch don’t fix the cause.

exam.q: Which artefact set should an LLMOps pipeline version and test, in addition to code?
o: Only the model weights, since everything else is configuration
Prompts, retrieval indexes, guardrail settings and tool definitions
The marketing materials that describe the application to customers
The personal laptops and phones used by the development team
exam.why: These artefacts change behaviour as much as code or model weights, so they need versioning, testing and approval.

exam.q: A research team runs Jupyter notebooks on a server reachable from the internet, with a shared administrator token and production database credentials stored in notebook cells. Which change is MOST important FIRST?
o: Upgrade the server’s GPUs, to improve the speed of everyone’s experiments
Remove internet exposure, rotate credentials, require individual logins
Ask researchers to delete any old notebooks they no longer use
Add a warning banner to the notebook server’s login page
exam.why: Internet exposure with a shared token and stored production credentials is an open door: close it, rotate the exposed credentials and require individual authentication.

exam.q: An agent that executes generated code runs in the same network as internal databases. Which environmental control BEST reduces the risk?
o: Giving the agent read-only database credentials instead of write access
A sandbox isolated from internal networks and secrets, with egress limits
Asking the model to avoid generating code that connects to databases
Logging all code the agent runs for review at the end of each month
exam.why: Isolation removes the paths a manipulated agent could use. Read-only credentials still allow data theft, instructions to the model are weak, and monthly reviews are too late.

exam.q: A provider announces it will retire the model version an application uses. The team plans to switch to the provider’s newest model the day before retirement. What should change management require?
o: Nothing, because the provider has tested the new model thoroughly
Comparative evaluation and approval well ahead, with a rollback plan
A contract clause preventing the provider from ever retiring models
Rebuilding the application from scratch around a different provider
exam.why: A provider model change is a behaviour change: evaluate it against the current version early, approve it by risk and keep a fallback. The other options are unrealistic or disproportionate.

exam.q: A team loosened a guardrail threshold to reduce customer complaints, treating it as a minor configuration tweak with no review. What does this indicate?
o: Good agility, since guardrails should be tuned freely by any engineer
A behaviour-changing change made without impact analysis or approval
A problem with the customers, who should accept the guardrail’s decisions
Nothing of concern, as guardrail thresholds don’t affect security
exam.why: Guardrail thresholds directly affect safety and security, so changes need impact analysis, evaluation and approval.

exam.q: Under the EU AI Act, why might a major update to a high-risk AI system need special attention in change management?
o: Updates to high-risk systems are prohibited once they are on the market
A substantial modification can trigger a new conformity assessment
High-risk systems may only be updated once every three years
The Act requires all updates to be approved by the European Commission
exam.why: Substantial modifications can require a new conformity assessment, so impact analysis must consider regulatory as well as technical effects.

exam.q: A bank releases a new credit model to 5% of applicants first, watching approval rates by group, error rates and complaints, with automatic reversion if any breach agreed limits. Which practice is this?
o: A blue-green deployment with an instant full switch
A canary release with pre-agreed rollback triggers
A shadow deployment, since only some applicants are affected
A ring deployment limited to internal staff
exam.why: A small share of real traffic, with monitored signals and automatic reversion, is a canary with rollback triggers. Shadow mode wouldn’t affect real applicants.

exam.q: After a rollback, an agent keeps behaving like the new version for some users. Investigation shows the new version wrote instructions into users’ persistent memory. What should the rollback procedure have included?
o: Rolling back the model only, since memory doesn’t affect behaviour
Handling state: reverting or cleaning memory written by the new version
Deleting all users’ accounts, so that they start again from scratch
Waiting for the memory entries to expire naturally over several months
exam.why: Rollbacks must handle state that the new version created, such as memory, caches and data changes, or the old behaviour won’t fully return.
